structure.title: Books 1–2 · Quarrel in the camp
structure.text: The Greeks are already at Troy. A plague forces Agamemnon to give up a captive woman, and he compensates himself at Achilles' expense. When their best fighter withdraws, thousands of men who had no say in the quarrel must bear its cost.

structure.title: Books 3–8 · What the armies are fighting over
structure.text: Duels briefly promise to settle the war. Between encounters the poem crosses the walls into Troy, where Hector meets a wife and child who stand to lose absolutely everything if the men outside prevail.

structure.title: Books 9–18 · What could bring a man back?
structure.text: Gifts and speeches fail to resolve the insult. As the fighting reaches the Greek ships, Patroclus asks for a particular concession. Achilles must discover where a friend's exposure to danger leaves his own refusal to fight.

structure.title: Books 19–24 · What the living owe the dead
structure.text: Achilles' return changes the balance of the fighting. Yet the poem gives its last stretch to other kinds of action as well, including funeral games, an old man's journey and negotiations over a body.

people.name: Achilles and Agamemnon
people.text: One supplies the army's greatest fighting strength. The other distributes its prizes. Their quarrel tests how far either kind of authority can go when its holder needs the other man's cooperation.

people.name: Hector and Andromache
people.text: His standing in the city depends upon meeting the Greeks outside its walls. She can picture in detail what losing him would mean, because war has already taken the rest of her family.

context.title: What a prize proclaims
context.text: A share of captured wealth publicly measures a warrior's standing. Taking Briseis from Achilles announces to every witness whose service can be slighted. She too has a history of losses, which becomes audible when she has occasion to mourn.

context.title: The war is old when the poem starts
context.text: Helen is already in Troy, and the Greek army has spent years in camp. The poem chooses a short span around Achilles’ anger. Stories of earlier courtships and expeditions enter when someone remembers them or needs them in an argument.

notice.text: Notice the lives compressed into a few lines before a death.
notice.why: A father, occupation or home river can suddenly come into view. Someone barely distinguishable in the battle line was somebody quite specific in the place he came from.

notice.text: Follow the comparisons beyond the battlefield.
notice.why: Shepherds, harvests and animals interrupt the fighting. Their details can make violence easier to picture while recalling the ordinary world that gets very little protection from it.

opening: Achilles refuses to fight because his commander has humiliated him. He is the army's best warrior, and he wants the Greeks to discover how badly they need him, even if that means watching them die. Across the battlefield, Hector returns briefly to his wife and child before going out again. Homer gives both armies people worth mourning. The glory is real, but so are the bodies, and a man's wounded pride can become a disaster that thousands of families have to live through.
